newsitem.title: USA: Parents to spend less as teens kick in for back-to-school.
newsitem.headline: Parents to spend less as teens kick in for back-to-school.

text.p: The back-to-school shopping season is right around the corner and despite all the spiral notebooks, jeans and gym socks parents will buy, there is some good news.
Parents can expect to spend significantly less this year than they did last year -- about 15 percent less -- for their children's clothing and school supplies.

According to the 1997 American Express Retail Index on back-to-school shopping, which monitors consumer spending, teenagers and parents will spend a combined average of $396 on back-to-school items this year.
Parents will pick up the majority of the cost, spending an average of $307, with teenagers contributing another $89.
Last year, parents alone expected to pay $363 per child and said their teenagers' financial contribution would be too insignificant to include.
Part of the decline in parents' spending in 1997 relects the overall slowing of growth in retail spending, an Amex spokesman said.

On Tuesday, the Commerce Department said sales at retail stores picked up more strongly than expected in June following three straight monthly declines. Total retail sales increased last month by 0.5 percent to a seasonally adjusted $210.3 billion after a revised 0.3 percent drop in May.

Industry reports from chain stores that sell everything from clothing to general merchandise had already indicated some improvement in business last month, Commerce said, though analysts noted that many stores heavily discounted prices to boost sales.
The decline in spending by parents noted in the Amex survey also shows that parents are expecting their teenagers to contribute more for their school needs.

The mad dash to buy school stuff before the term starts is a fact of life for 98 percent of back-to-schoolers, but 60 percent will continue to shop after the fall semester begins. Reasons include time constraints, seasonal fashion changes and a desire to see what is popular.
Girls surveyed said they plan to update their school wardrobe an average of nine times during the school year, while boys plan to shop only five additional times.

The survey by the financial services company of 1,000 adults and children indicates that while 9l percent of teenagers do not have to wear a school-sanctioned uniform, there is often an informal "uniform" when it comes to clothing preferences.
More than 75 percent of teenagerss surveyed expect to buy jeans or denim pants and, of these, 86 percent want loose-fitting jeans and 80 percent prefer blue over any other colour.

Overall, 83 percent of teenagers said they set their own fashion styles, while elementary school students said they were more influenced by sports figures, television, musical artists and their siblings.

Levi's were cited as the brand of choice by 40 percent of teenagers, down only slightly from 45 percent in 1996. Calvin Klein came in a distant second preference for high school and college students, at 10 percent. Arizona jeans made by J.C. Penney is the second most popular choice for grade-schoolers, American Express said.
Nike-branded clothes, which was No. 2 last year, was not among this year's top five.

According to the survey, the top five clothing brands for elementary school-aged girls are: Calvin Klein (42 percent), Levi's (38 percent), The Gap (38 percent), Tommy Hilfiger (29 percent) and Guess (20 percent). Boys prefer Levi's (40 percent), Tommy Hilfiger (31 percent), Calvin Klein (22 percent), Polo/Ralph Lauren (21 percent), and The Gap (16 percent).
Over two-thirds (66 percent) of parents of high-schoolers described their child as "extremely" style-conscious, which, Amex said, contributed to the renewed popularity of shopping malls.
"This year's survey of teens and parents helps explain the popularity of shopping malls," said Emelie Smith, vice president, Retail Marketing Group, American Express Travel Related Services.
"The great advantage of malls is they satisfy a teen's need for an endless choice of brands and styles, while appealing to their parents' desire for convenient comparison shopping," she said.
About 30 percent of parents said malls were where they will do most of their back-to-school shopping, compared with 79 percent of teens.
Discount department stores, which were the most popular retailers cited by parents surveyed in 1996, was the second most popular retail outlet this year, chosen by 23 percent.

When it comes to paying for purchases, cash is still No. 1. Most back-to-school purchases (62 percent) will be paid for in cash. Personal checks will account for about 13 percent of spending and credit or charge chards will account for about 12 percent. Last year, the percentages were slightly higher in each category, due to changes in survey techniques, an Amex spokesman said.

Parents of college-aged students are expected to use credit cards more often (22 percent) than parents of elementary school students (8 percent). Amex theorised that this difference can be attributed to the more expensive items college students need, such as small appliances, furniture, and textbooks.

In addition to apparel, which appears on 87 percent of all back-to-school shopping lists, parents and teenagers plan to buy school supplies (85 percent), textbooks (41 percent), sporting goods (26 percent), computer hardware and software (24 percent), small appliances/electronics (11 percent), and furniture (5 percent).
